title: Taylor Chapter 13: Hamiltonian Mechanics
text:
According to the PHY C54 Syllabus, Hamiltonian Mechanics spans Week 04 (Ch 13: 1–4) and Week 05 (Ch 13: 5–7), concluding before Test #1.



The Legendre Transformation: Transitioning from generalized velocities \(\dot{q}_i\) to generalized canonical momenta \(p_i = \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \dot{q}_i}\).
Hamilton’s Canonical Equations: \[ \dot{q}_i = \frac{\partial \mathcal{H}}{\partial p_i}, \quad \dot{p}_i = -\frac{\partial \mathcal{H}}{\partial q_i} \]
Phase Space Geometry & Liouville’s Theorem: Incompressibility of phase space volume under Hamiltonian time evolution (\(\frac{d\rho}{dt} = 0\)).
Poisson Brackets: Fundamental brackets, equations of motion in Poisson form, and canonical invariance: \[ [F, G] = \sum_i \left( \frac{\partial F}{\partial q_i}\frac{\partial G}{\partial p_i} - \frac{\partial F}{\partial p_i}\frac{\partial G}{\partial q_i} \right) \]
Noether’s Theorem in Hamiltonian Mechanics: Symmetries, generators of infinitesimal canonical transformations, and conservation laws.

title: Taylor Chapter 10: Rotational Motion of Rigid Bodies
text:
According to the PHY C54 Syllabus, Rigid Body Dynamics is studied in Weeks 09, 10, and 11 (Taylor Ch 10: 1–10), following Test #2.



Center of Mass & Angular Momentum: \(\mathbf{L} = \sum_\alpha \mathbf{r}_\alpha \times \mathbf{p}_\alpha = \mathbf{I}\boldsymbol{\omega}\).

title: Taylor Chapter 7: Lagrange’s Equations
text:
The theoretical development of the laws of motion found its most poetic formulation in 1788 when the Italian-French mathematician Joseph-Louis Lagrange published Mécanique Analytique.
The Lagrangian formulation holds two major advantages over Newtonian mechanics: 1. Lagrange’s equations take the same form in any coordinate system (Cartesian, spherical, non-inertial, etc.). 2. For constrained systems (like a bead on a wire), the Lagrangian approach naturally eliminates the forces of constraint (like normal forces), which are often unknown and uninteresting.



(See Problems 7.1-7.7)
For a particle moving freely in 3D subject to a conservative force \(\mathbf{F} = -\nabla U\), the Lagrangian \(\mathcal{L}\) is defined as the kinetic energy minus the potential energy: \[ \mathcal{L} = T - U = \frac{1}{2}m(\dot{x}^2 + \dot{y}^2 + \dot{z}^2) - U(x, y, z) \]
By checking the partial derivatives, we see that: \[ \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial x} = -\frac{\partial U}{\partial x} = F_x, \quad \text{and} \quad \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \dot{x}} = m\dot{x} = p_x \] Newton’s second law (\(F_x = \dot{p}_x\)) is therefore exactly equivalent to the Lagrange equation in Cartesian coordinates: \[ \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial x} - \frac{d}{dt}\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \dot{x}} = 0 \]


Because this has the exact form of the Euler-Lagrange equations, we can re-state Newton’s Second Law as an integral variational principle known as Hamilton’s Principle: > The actual path which a particle follows between two points 1 and 2 in a given time interval makes the action integral \(S = \int_{t_1}^{t_2} \mathcal{L} \, dt\) stationary.
Because Hamilton’s Principle applies globally to the action integral \(S\), the value of the integral is invariant under coordinate transformations. This proves that Lagrange’s equations are valid in any choice of generalized coordinates \(q_1, q_2, \dots, q_n\).



If we write \(\mathcal{L} = \frac{1}{2}m(\dot{r}^2 + r^2 \dot{\theta}^2) - U(r, \theta)\), the \(\theta\) equation becomes: \[ \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \theta} = \frac{d}{dt} \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \dot{\theta}} \implies -\frac{\partial U}{\partial \theta} = \frac{d}{dt} (mr^2 \dot{\theta}) \] Since \(-\partial U/\partial \theta\) is the torque \(\Gamma\) and \(mr^2\dot{\theta}\) is the angular momentum \(L\), this automatically yields \(\Gamma = \dot{L}\). The geometry of the coordinates naturally yields the appropriate mechanical theorem.





(See Problems 7.9-7.11)
A system of \(N\) particles with positions \(\mathbf{r}_\alpha\) is parametrized by generalized coordinates \(q_1, \dots, q_n\): \[ \mathbf{r}_\alpha = \mathbf{r}_\alpha(q_1, \dots, q_n, t) \]

Degrees of Freedom: The number of independently variable coordinates \(n\). If \(n < 3N\), the system is constrained.
Holonomic Systems: When the number of degrees of freedom exactly matches the number of generalized coordinates required to describe the configuration, the system is holonomic. (A rolling ball is non-holonomic, as it needs 5 coordinates but only has 2 translational degrees of freedom).
Natural Coordinates: If the transformation mapping \(\mathbf{r}_\alpha(q_1, \dots, q_n)\) does not depend explicitly on time \(t\), the coordinates are called “natural”.





(See Problems 7.12-7.13)
For a particle constrained to a surface (e.g., a bead on a wire), the total force is \(\mathbf{F}_{tot} = \mathbf{F}_{cstr} + \mathbf{F}\). The constraint force \(\mathbf{F}_{cstr}\) acts normal to the surface, and any virtual displacement \(\epsilon\) consistent with the constraint lies within the surface. Thus, \(\mathbf{F}_{cstr} \cdot \epsilon = 0\).
This geometric fact means the constraint forces do zero virtual work, entirely vanishing from the variation of the action \(\delta S = 0\). The resulting path requires only the potential \(U\) of the non-constraint forces: \[ \mathcal{L}(q, \dot{q}, t) = T - U \] yielding the \(n\) equations of motion: \[ \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial q_i} - \frac{d}{dt}\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \dot{q}_i} = 0 \quad \text{for } i = 1, \dots, n \]




(See Problems 7.14-7.44)
The procedure is nearly infallible: 1. Choose \(n\) generalized coordinates. 2. Write \(T\) and \(U\) in an inertial frame, then express them in terms of the \(q\)’s and \(\dot{q}\)’s. 3. Construct \(\mathcal{L} = T - U\). 4. Evaluate the Lagrange equations.


Consider a circular wire hoop of radius \(R\) spinning at constant angular velocity \(\omega\) about its vertical axis, with a bead of mass \(m\) free to slide. The generalized coordinate is the angle \(\theta\) from the bottom.
\[ \mathcal{L} = \frac{1}{2}mR^2(\dot{\theta}^2 + \omega^2 \sin^2 \theta) - mgR(1 - \cos \theta) \] The equation of motion is: \[ R\ddot{\theta} = (\omega^2 R \cos \theta - g) \sin \theta \]
When \(\omega^2 < g/R\), the only stable equilibrium is at the bottom (\(\theta=0\)). But when the hoop spins fast enough (\(\omega^2 > g/R\)), the bottom becomes an unstable equilibrium, and two new stable equilibria emerge at \(\theta = \pm \arccos(g / \omega^2 R)\). This emergence is known in chaos theory as a pitchfork bifurcation.


Code
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

theta = np.linspace(-np.pi, np.pi, 200)
R = 1.0
g = 9.81

plt.figure(figsize=(8, 4))
for w_sq in [5, 9.81, 20, 40]:
    force = (w_sq * R * np.cos(theta) - g) * np.sin(theta)
    plt.plot(theta, force, label=rf'$\omega^2={w_sq}$')

plt.axhline(0, color='k', linestyle='--', linewidth=0.8)
plt.title("Restoring Force vs. Angle $\\theta$")
plt.xlabel("$\\theta$ (radians)")
plt.ylabel("Normalized Force")
plt.legend()
plt.grid(True)
plt.show()








Figure 1: The effective restoring force on the spinning hoop bead. Note the stable equilibria moving away from the origin as rotation rate increases.










We define the generalized force \(F_i\) and generalized momentum \(p_i\) as: \[ F_i = \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial q_i} \quad \text{and} \quad p_i = \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \dot{q}_i} \] Lagrange’s equations become exactly \(F_i = \dot{p}_i\).
Ignorable Coordinates: If \(\mathcal{L}\) is independent of a coordinate \(q_k\), we call \(q_k\) ignorable or cyclic. Its generalized force \(F_k = 0\), meaning the conjugate momentum \(p_k\) is strictly conserved! Every ignorable coordinate points to a conservation law.




(See Problems 7.45-7.47)


If an isolated system is translationally invariant (meaning \(\mathcal{L}\) doesn’t change if we shift all particles by an infinitesimal vector \(\boldsymbol{\epsilon}\)), it follows directly from Lagrange’s equations that the total linear momentum \(\mathbf{P} = \sum \mathbf{p}_\alpha\) is conserved.



The total time derivative of \(\mathcal{L}\) leads us to define the Hamiltonian \(\mathcal{H}\): \[ \mathcal{H} = \sum_{i=1}^n p_i \dot{q}_i - \mathcal{L} \]
If the Lagrangian has no explicit time dependence (\(\partial \mathcal{L} / \partial t = 0\)), then \(d\mathcal{H}/dt = 0\), and the Hamiltonian is conserved. Furthermore, if the generalized coordinates are natural (time-independent transformations), Euler’s homogeneous function theorem guarantees that the kinetic energy \(T\) is a homogeneous quadratic function of the velocities, which implies: \[ \sum_{i} p_i \dot{q}_i = 2T \implies \mathcal{H} = 2T - (T - U) = T + U = E \] Hence, time-translation invariance leads to Energy Conservation.





(See Problems 7.48-7.49)
For a charged particle \(q\) in an electromagnetic field described by a scalar potential \(V\) and vector potential \(\mathbf{A}\), the Lorentz force is velocity-dependent: \(\mathbf{F} = q(\mathbf{E} + \mathbf{v} \times \mathbf{B})\).
The Lagrangian formulation still works if we adopt a generalized definition of the Lagrangian—a Lagrangian is simply any scalar function \(\mathcal{L}\) that reproduces the correct equations of motion.
For the electromagnetic case, the correct function is: \[ \mathcal{L} = \frac{1}{2}m\dot{\mathbf{r}}^2 - q(V - \dot{\mathbf{r}} \cdot \mathbf{A}) \] This Lagrangian is foundational to quantum mechanics, as it modifies the canonical generalized momentum of the particle: \[ \mathbf{p} = \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \dot{\mathbf{r}}} = m\mathbf{v} + q\mathbf{A} \] This shows that the momentum operator in quantum mechanics corresponds to \(m\mathbf{v} + q\mathbf{A}\), not just the mechanical momentum \(m\mathbf{v}\).




(See Problems 7.50-7.52)
If we need to determine a constraint force (e.g. tension in a string, or structural stress on a roller coaster track), we deliberately don’t use a minimal set of coordinates. Instead, we retain extra coordinates tied by a constraint equation \(f(q_1, q_2) = \text{const}\).
We introduce a Lagrange multiplier \(\lambda(t)\) to scale the constraint equation, modifying Hamilton’s principle: \[ \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial q_i} - \frac{d}{dt}\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \dot{q}_i} + \lambda \frac{\partial f}{\partial q_i} = 0 \]
The extra term \(\lambda \frac{\partial f}{\partial q_i}\) is precisely the \(i\)-th component of the force of constraint. Solving this system of differential algebraic equations (DAEs) yields both the trajectory \(q_i(t)\) and the dynamic magnitude of the constraint force via \(\lambda(t)\).

title: Vector Calculus & Identities
text:

\[ \mathbf{A} \cdot \mathbf{B} = A_x B_x + A_y B_y + A_z B_z = |\mathbf{A}| |\mathbf{B}| \cos\theta \] \[ \mathbf{A} \times \mathbf{B} = \det \begin{vmatrix} \mathbf{\hat{i}} & \mathbf{\hat{j}} & \mathbf{\hat{k}} \\ A_x & A_y & A_z \\ B_x & B_y & B_z \end{vmatrix} \] \[ |\mathbf{A} \times \mathbf{B}| = |\mathbf{A}| |\mathbf{B}| \sin\theta \]

title: Computational Methods for Mechanics
text:
In classical mechanics, analytic solutions are often impossible for systems that exhibit nonlinear dynamics, chaos, or lack conservation laws (e.g., the double pendulum, the 3-body problem, or driven damped oscillators). For these, we rely on numerical integration of Ordinary Differential Equations (ODEs).
Any \(n\)-th order ODE can be reduced to a system of \(n\) first-order ODEs. For Newton’s second law \(\ddot{\mathbf{x}} = \mathbf{F}(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{v}, t)/m\), we define the state vector \(\mathbf{Y} = [\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{v}]^T\): \[ \frac{d\mathbf{Y}}{dt} = \begin{bmatrix} \mathbf{v} \\ \mathbf{a} \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} \mathbf{v} \\ \mathbf{F}/m \end{bmatrix} \]

title: Computational Methods for Mechanics
text:
The Velocity Verlet Method
Used extensively in molecular dynamics and astrophysics: 1. Update position by a half-step and full-step acceleration: \[ \mathbf{x}_{n+1} = \mathbf{x}_n + \mathbf{v}_n \Delta t + \frac{1}{2}\mathbf{a}_n \Delta t^2 \] 2. Calculate new forces/accelerations based on new position: \[ \mathbf{a}_{n+1} = \frac{1}{m} \mathbf{F}(\mathbf{x}_{n+1}) \] 3. Update velocity using the average of old and new accelerations: \[ \mathbf{v}_{n+1} = \mathbf{v}_n + \frac{1}{2}(\mathbf{a}_n + \mathbf{a}_{n+1}) \Delta t \]


Code
import numpy as np

def velocity_verlet(x0, v0, force_func, m, dt, steps):
    x = np.zeros(steps)
    v = np.zeros(steps)
    x[0], v[0] = x0, v0
    
    a = force_func(x0) / m
    for i in range(steps - 1):
        x[i+1] = x[i] + v[i]*dt + 0.5*a*dt**2
        a_next = force_func(x[i+1]) / m
        v[i+1] = v[i] + 0.5*(a + a_next)*dt
        a = a_next
        
    return x, v

title: Taylor Chapter 7 Problems: Lagrange’s Equations
text:
This article contains problem statements and solution outlines for Chapter 7 of John R. Taylor’s Classical Mechanics. For a theoretical overview, see the Chapter 7 Lecture Notes.




Statement: Write down the Lagrangian for a projectile (subject to no air resistance) in terms of its Cartesian coordinates \((x, y, z)\), with \(z\) measured vertically upward. Find the three Lagrange equations and show that they are exactly what you would expect.
(See Section 7.1 Notes)
Solution: \(\mathcal{L} = \frac{1}{2}m(\dot{x}^2 + \dot{y}^2 + \dot{z}^2) - mgz\). The equations are: - \(x\): \(\frac{d}{dt}(m\dot{x}) = 0 \implies \ddot{x} = 0\) - \(y\): \(\frac{d}{dt}(m\dot{y}) = 0 \implies \ddot{y} = 0\) - \(z\): \(\frac{d}{dt}(m\dot{z}) = -mg \implies \ddot{z} = -g\) These are the standard equations of motion for a projectile.



Statement: Write down the Lagrangian for a one-dimensional particle moving along the \(x\) axis and subject to a force \(F = -kx\) (with \(k\) positive). Find the Lagrange equation of motion and solve it.
Solution: \(\mathcal{L} = \frac{1}{2}m\dot{x}^2 - \frac{1}{2}kx^2\). Equation: \(-kx = m\ddot{x} \implies \ddot{x} + \omega^2 x = 0\). Solution is simple harmonic motion \(x(t) = A\cos(\omega t - \delta)\).



Statement: Consider a mass \(m\) moving in two dimensions with potential energy \(U(x, y) = \frac{1}{2}kr^2\), where \(r^2 = x^2 + y^2\). Write down the Lagrangian and find the two Lagrange equations of motion. Describe their solutions.
Solution: \(\mathcal{L} = \frac{1}{2}m(\dot{x}^2 + \dot{y}^2) - \frac{1}{2}k(x^2 + y^2)\). Equations: \(m\ddot{x} = -kx\) and \(m\ddot{y} = -ky\). Both \(x\) and \(y\) undergo independent simple harmonic motion with the same frequency.



Statement: Mass \(m\) moving in a frictionless plane that slopes at angle \(\alpha\). Write down the Lagrangian in terms of \(x\) (horizontally across slope) and \(y\) (down slope).
Solution: \(\mathcal{L} = \frac{1}{2}m(\dot{x}^2 + \dot{y}^2) + mgy\sin\alpha\). Equations: \(m\ddot{x} = 0\) and \(m\ddot{y} = mg\sin\alpha\).



Statement: Show that the \(3N\) Newtonian equations are exactly equivalent to the \(3N\) Lagrange equations in Cartesian coordinates, establishing Hamilton’s principle.






Statement: Bead threaded on a rigid circular hoop of radius \(R\) in the \(xy\) plane. Use the angle \(\phi\). Write equations giving \((x, y)\) in terms of \(\phi\).
(See Section 7.3 Notes)
Solution: \(x = R\cos\phi, \quad y = R\sin\phi\). Generalized coordinate is just \(\phi\).



Statement: Particle on the surface of a circular cone, axis on \(z\), half-angle \(\alpha\).
Solution: Using cylindrical \(( \rho, \phi, z )\): \(z = \rho \cot \alpha\). The coordinates are \((\rho, \phi)\). \(x = \rho\cos\phi\), \(y = \rho\sin\phi\), \(z = \rho\cot\alpha\).






Statement: Modify Lagrange’s equations to include a nonconservative force \(F_{\text{fric}}\).
(See Section 7.4 Notes)
Solution: \(\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial x} + F_{\text{fric}} = \frac{d}{dt} \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \dot{x}}\).



Statement: Prove Lagrange’s equations for two particles subject to various constraints, using the property that constraint forces do zero net work.






Statement: Massless string wrapped around a uniform cylinder (mass \(m\), radius \(R\)). Find acceleration.
Solution: \(\mathcal{L} = \frac{1}{2}m\dot{x}^2 + \frac{1}{2}(\frac{1}{2}mR^2)\omega^2 - (-mgx)\). Since \(x = R\phi\), \(\omega = \dot{x}/R\). \(\mathcal{L} = \frac{3}{4}m\dot{x}^2 + mgx\). Equation: \(mg = \frac{3}{2}m\ddot{x} \implies \ddot{x} = \frac{2}{3}g\).



(Standard problems: Mass on table attached to hanging mass, Cylinder rolling down incline, Atwood machine with massive pulley).



Statement: Rod forced to rotate in horizontal plane at constant \(\omega\). Bead on rod.
Solution: \(\mathcal{L} = \frac{1}{2}m(\dot{r}^2 + r^2\omega^2)\). Equation: \(m\ddot{r} = mr\omega^2\). Shows centrifugal force accelerating the bead exponentially.



(Problems verifying stable/unstable equilibria and normal mode frequencies for rotating systems and pendulums attached to wheels.)






Statement: Prove that rotational invariance of \(\mathcal{L}\) implies conservation of total angular momentum.
(See Section 7.8 Notes)
Solution: Rotating by \(\epsilon\) around the \(z\)-axis changes coordinates. If \(\delta \mathcal{L} = 0\), the sum of \(\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \phi_\alpha} = 0 \implies \sum \dot{p}_{\phi_\alpha} = 0 \implies L_z\) is conserved.






Statement: Charge \(q\) in uniform magnetic field \(B \hat{z}\). Prove \(B = \nabla \times A\) and find Lagrange equations.
(See Section 7.9 Notes)
Solution: \(A = \frac{1}{2} B \times r\). The Lagrangian involves the vector potential, leading directly to the Lorentz force equation.






Statement: Atwood machine and pendulum solved using Lagrange multipliers \(\lambda\) to find string tensions.
(See Section 7.10 Notes)
Solution: For the pendulum, constraint \(f(x, y) = \sqrt{x^2 + y^2} = l\). The multiplier \(\lambda\) represents the constraint force (tension), yielding equations that simultaneously solve the motion and the dynamic tension in the rod.

title: Problem Set 1: Bead on a Rotating Wire Hoop
text:
Solution

1. Constructing the Lagrangian
Let \(\theta\) be the angle of the bead measured from the lowest point of the hoop. In spherical coordinates with the origin at the center of the hoop: * \(x = R \sin\theta \cos(\omega t)\) * \(y = R \sin\theta \sin(\omega t)\) * \(z = -R \cos\theta\)
Taking time derivatives: \[\dot{x} = R \dot{\theta} \cos\theta \cos(\omega t) - R \omega \sin\theta \sin(\omega t)\] \[\dot{y} = R \dot{\theta} \cos\theta \sin(\omega t) + R \omega \sin\theta \cos(\omega t)\] \[\dot{z} = R \dot{\theta} \sin\theta\]
Calculating \(v^2 = \dot{x}^2 + \dot{y}^2 + \dot{z}^2\): \[v^2 = R^2 \dot{\theta}^2 + R^2 \omega^2 \sin^2\theta\]

Kinetic Energy: \(T = \frac{1}{2} m R^2 (\dot{\theta}^2 + \omega^2 \sin^2\theta)\)
Potential Energy: \(V = mgz = -mgR \cos\theta\)

The Lagrangian is: \[\boxed{\mathcal{L} = T - V = \frac{1}{2} m R^2 \dot{\theta}^2 + \frac{1}{2} m R^2 \omega^2 \sin^2\theta + mgR \cos\theta}\]



2. Equation of Motion
Compute the Euler-Lagrange derivatives: \[\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \dot{\theta}} = m R^2 \dot{\theta} \implies \frac{d}{dt}\left(\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \dot{\theta}}\right) = m R^2 \ddot{\theta}\] \[\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \theta} = m R^2 \omega^2 \sin\theta \cos\theta - mgR \sin\theta\]
Applying \(\frac{d}{dt}\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \dot{\theta}} - \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \theta} = 0\): \[m R^2 \ddot{\theta} - m R^2 \omega^2 \sin\theta \cos\theta + mgR \sin\theta = 0\] \[\boxed{\ddot{\theta} = \left( \omega^2 \cos\theta - \frac{g}{R} \right) \sin\theta}\]



3. Equilibrium Positions and Stability Analysis
Equilibrium occurs when \(\ddot{\theta} = 0\): \[\sin\theta \left( \omega^2 \cos\theta - \frac{g}{R} \right) = 0\]
This yields two distinct branches of equilibria: 1. \(\sin\theta = 0 \implies \theta_0 = 0\) (bottom) or \(\theta_0 = \pi\) (top). 2. \(\cos\theta_0 = \frac{g}{\omega^2 R}\) (lateral positions, existing only if \(\omega^2 \ge g/R\)).

Effective Potential
Rewrite the equation of motion as \(\ddot{\theta} = -\frac{1}{mR^2} \frac{dV_{\text{eff}}}{d\theta}\): \[V_{\text{eff}}(\theta) = -mgR \cos\theta - \frac{1}{2} m R^2 \omega^2 \sin^2\theta\]
Evaluate the second derivative \(\frac{d^2 V_{\text{eff}}}{d\theta^2}\): \[\frac{d^2 V_{\text{eff}}}{d\theta^2} = mgR \cos\theta - m R^2 \omega^2 \cos(2\theta)\]
At the bottom (\(\theta = 0\)): \[\left. \frac{d^2 V_{\text{eff}}}{d\theta^2} \right|_{\theta=0} = mgR - m R^2 \omega^2 = m R^2 \left( \frac{g}{R} - \omega^2 \right)\]

Subcritical (\(\omega < \sqrt{g/R}\)): \(V_{\text{eff}}''(0) > 0 \implies\) Stable minimum.
Supercritical (\(\omega > \sqrt{g/R}\)): \(V_{\text{eff}}''(0) < 0 \implies\) Unstable maximum. The bottom position loses stability!

At the critical rotation speed \(\omega_c = \sqrt{g/R}\), the system undergoes a classic supercritical pitchfork bifurcation: the bottom point becomes unstable, and two symmetric stable equilibrium points emerge at: \[\boxed{\theta_0 = \pm \arccos\left(\frac{g}{\omega^2 R}\right)}\]

Problem 6.1
The shortest path between two points on a curved surface, such as the surface of a sphere, is called a geodesic. 4. Fortran 90 Symplectic Orbit Integrator
For ultra-high-throughput orbital mechanics, Fortran remains an industry standard in celestial dynamics:
! orbit_integrator.f90
! Compile: gfortran -O3 -march=native orbit_integrator.f90 -o orbit_sim
program kepler_verlet
    implicit none
    integer, parameter :: dp = kind(1.0d0)
    real(dp) :: x, y, vx, vy, ax, ay, r, dt, t, t_end, GM
    real(dp) :: ax_new, ay_new
    integer :: step, n_steps

    GM = 4.0_dp * 3.141592653589793_dp**2 ! AU^3 / yr^2
    x = 1.0_dp; y = 0.0_dp               ! Initial position (1 AU)
    vx = 0.0_dp; vy = 2.0_dp * 3.141592653589793_dp ! Circular velocity

    dt = 0.001_dp
    t_end = 10.0_dp
    n_steps = int(t_end / dt)

    do step = 1, n_steps
        r = sqrt(x**2 + y**2)
        ax = -GM * x / (r**3)
        ay = -GM * y / (r**3)

        x = x + vx * dt + 0.5_dp * ax * dt**2
        y = y + vy * dt + 0.5_dp * ay * dt**2

        r = sqrt(x**2 + y**2)
        ax_new = -GM * x / (r**3)
        ay_new = -GM * y / (r**3)

        vx = vx + 0.5_dp * (ax + ax_new) * dt
        vy = vy + 0.5_dp * (ay + ay_new) * dt
    end do

    print *, "Completed 10 Earth orbits with zero secular energy drift."
end program kepler_verlet

title: Taylor Chapter 6: Calculus of Variations
text:
In classical mechanics, we often encounter problems where we need to find a path or a function that minimizes (or maximizes) a certain quantity. This is the domain of the Calculus of Variations. While ordinary calculus deals with finding points that extremize a function \(y = f(x)\), the calculus of variations deals with finding functions \(y(x)\) that extremize a functional (a function of a function), often expressed as an integral:
\[ S = \int_{x_1}^{x_2} f(y, y', x) \, dx \]
Two main classes of problems require this approach: 1. Symmetries make non-Cartesian coordinates (spherical, cylindrical) advantageous. 2. Constraints make it best to choose generalized coordinates (e.g., a particle on a sphere).
To transition to these generalized coordinates, Lagrangian mechanics provides a powerful framework built entirely on the calculus of variations and Hamilton’s Principle of Least Action.




What is the shortest path between two points \((x_1, y_1)\) and \((x_2, y_2)\) in a plane? Let the path be given by a function \(y = y(x)\). An infinitesimal element of length along the path is \(ds = \sqrt{dx^2 + dy^2} = \sqrt{1 + (y')^2} \, dx\), where \(y' = dy/dx\).
The total length of the path is the integral: \[ L = \int_{x_1}^{x_2} \sqrt{1 + [y'(x)]^2} \, dx \]
The goal is to find the function \(y(x)\) that minimizes \(L\).

Problem 6.1 (Shortest path in a plane): Prove that the shortest path between two points in a 2D plane is a straight line. (We will solve this using the Euler-Lagrange equation later in this chapter.)




First posed by Johann Bernoulli in 1696. Given two points 1 and 2, with 1 higher than 2, what is the shape of a frictionless wire connecting them such that a bead released from rest at 1 slides to 2 in the minimum possible time?
Let point 1 be the origin \((0,0)\). We take the \(y\)-axis pointing downward. The speed of the bead is \(v = ds/dt\). By conservation of energy, \(E = T + U\). If released from rest at \((0,0)\), \(E = 0\). \[ \frac{1}{2}mv^2 - mgy = 0 \implies v = \sqrt{2gy} \]
The time to travel an infinitesimal distance \(ds\) is \(dt = ds/v\). The total time is: \[ t = \int_{1}^{2} \frac{ds}{v} = \int_{x_1}^{x_2} \frac{\sqrt{1 + (y')^2}}{\sqrt{2gy}} \, dx \]
We need to find the function \(y(x)\) that minimizes this time integral \(t\).

Problem 6.2 (Brachistochrone coordinates): Write down the time integral if the \(y\)-axis was defined pointing upwards instead. How does the energy conservation equation change? Hint: If \(y\) points up, \(U = mgy\). \(E = 0 \implies \frac{1}{2}mv^2 + mgy = 0 \implies v = \sqrt{-2gy}\) (since \(y\) will be negative as the bead falls). The integral remains similar, just with \(-y\) under the square root.





Both examples above involve an integral of the form: \[ S[y] = \int_{x_1}^{x_2} f(y, y', x) \, dx \] where \(S\) is a functional. We want to find the path \(y(x)\) that makes \(S\) stationary (a minimum, maximum, or saddle point).


Let the actual path that extremizes the integral be \(y(x)\). Consider a “wrong” path \(Y(x)\) that is close to \(y(x)\). We can parameterize this wrong path as: \[ Y(x) = y(x) + \alpha \eta(x) \] where \(\alpha\) is a small parameter, and \(\eta(x)\) is an arbitrary differentiable function representing the variation. Since all paths must start at \(x_1\) and end at \(x_2\), the variation must vanish at the endpoints: \[ \eta(x_1) = \eta(x_2) = 0 \]
The integral evaluated along the varied path is a function of \(\alpha\): \[ S(\alpha) = \int_{x_1}^{x_2} f(Y, Y', x) \, dx = \int_{x_1}^{x_2} f(y + \alpha \eta, y' + \alpha \eta', x) \, dx \]
For the integral to be stationary at the correct path \(y(x)\), the derivative of \(S\) with respect to \(\alpha\) must be zero when \(\alpha = 0\): \[ \left. \frac{dS}{d\alpha} \right|_{\alpha=0} = 0 \]
Using the chain rule to differentiate inside the integral: \[ \frac{dS}{d\alpha} = \int_{x_1}^{x_2} \left( \frac{\partial f}{\partial Y} \frac{\partial Y}{\partial \alpha} + \frac{\partial f}{\partial Y'} \frac{\partial Y'}{\partial \alpha} \right) dx = \int_{x_1}^{x_2} \left( \frac{\partial f}{\partial Y} \eta + \frac{\partial f}{\partial Y'} \eta' \right) dx \]
Set \(\alpha = 0\), so \(Y \to y\) and \(Y' \to y'\): \[ \int_{x_1}^{x_2} \left( \frac{\partial f}{\partial y} \eta(x) + \frac{\partial f}{\partial y'} \eta'(x) \right) dx = 0 \]
We integrate the second term by parts: \[ \int_{x_1}^{x_2} \frac{\partial f}{\partial y'} \eta'(x) \, dx = \left[ \frac{\partial f}{\partial y'} \eta(x) \right]_{x_1}^{x_2} - \int_{x_1}^{x_2} \frac{d}{dx} \left( \frac{\partial f}{\partial y'} \right) \eta(x) \, dx \]
Since \(\eta(x_1) = \eta(x_2) = 0\), the boundary term vanishes. The condition becomes: \[ \int_{x_1}^{x_2} \left[ \frac{\partial f}{\partial y} - \frac{d}{dx} \left( \frac{\partial f}{\partial y'} \right) \right] \eta(x) \, dx = 0 \]
For this to hold for any arbitrary variation \(\eta(x)\), the term in the brackets must be identically zero. This yields the Euler-Lagrange Equation:
\[ \frac{\partial f}{\partial y} - \frac{d}{dx} \frac{\partial f}{\partial y'} = 0 \]

Problem 6.4: Find the Euler-Lagrange equation for the functional \(S = \int (y'^2 + y^2) dx\). Solution: \(f = y'^2 + y^2\). \(\frac{\partial f}{\partial y} = 2y\), \(\frac{\partial f}{\partial y'} = 2y'\). \(\frac{d}{dx}(2y') = 2y''\). The E-L equation is \(2y - 2y'' = 0\), or \(y'' = y\).







For the shortest path, \(f(y, y', x) = \sqrt{1 + y'^2}\). Since \(\partial f / \partial y = 0\), the E-L equation reduces to: \[ \frac{d}{dx} \left( \frac{\partial f}{\partial y'} \right) = 0 \implies \frac{\partial f}{\partial y'} = C \] \[ \frac{y'}{\sqrt{1 + y'^2}} = C \implies y'^2 = C^2(1 + y'^2) \implies y'^2 = \frac{C^2}{1-C^2} = m^2 \] Thus, \(y' = m\), meaning \(y = mx + b\). The shortest path is a straight line.



For the Brachistochrone, \(f = \sqrt{\frac{1+y'^2}{y}}\) (ignoring constants). Notice that \(f\) does not depend explicitly on \(x\). When \(\partial f / \partial x = 0\), we can use the Beltrami Identity (a first integral of the E-L equation): \[ f - y' \frac{\partial f}{\partial y'} = C \]
Substituting \(f\): \[ \sqrt{\frac{1+y'^2}{y}} - y' \frac{y'}{\sqrt{y(1+y'^2)}} = C \] \[ \frac{1+y'^2 - y'^2}{\sqrt{y(1+y'^2)}} = C \implies \frac{1}{\sqrt{y(1+y'^2)}} = C \implies y(1+y'^2) = \frac{1}{C^2} = 2a \]
Solving for \(y'\): \[ y' = \frac{dy}{dx} = \sqrt{\frac{2a-y}{y}} \implies dx = \sqrt{\frac{y}{2a-y}} dy \]
To integrate this, we use the substitution \(y = a(1 - \cos\theta)\). Then \(dy = a \sin\theta \, d\theta\). \[ dx = \sqrt{\frac{a(1-\cos\theta)}{a(1+\cos\theta)}} a \sin\theta \, d\theta = a (1-\cos\theta) d\theta \] Integrating gives the parametric equations for a cycloid: \[ x(\theta) = a(\theta - \sin\theta) \] \[ y(\theta) = a(1 - \cos\theta) \]


Code
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

theta = np.linspace(0, 2*np.pi, 100)
a = 1
x = a * (theta - np.sin(theta))
y = a * (1 - np.cos(theta)) # Positive downwards

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 4))
ax.plot(x, -y, label='Brachistochrone (Cycloid)', color='blue') # Negative to plot downwards intuitively
ax.plot([0, x[-1]], [0, -y[-1]], '--', label='Straight line', color='gray')
ax.set_aspect('equal')
ax.set_xlabel('x')
ax.set_ylabel('y')
ax.set_title('Path of Minimum Time (Brachistochrone)')
ax.legend()
plt.grid(True)
plt.show()








Figure 1: The Brachistochrone path is a cycloid, the curve traced by a point on the rim of a rolling wheel.






Problem 6.11 (Geodesic on a cylinder): Find the equation for the shortest path (geodesic) between two points on the surface of a cylinder \(R = \text{const}\). Hint: Use cylindrical coordinates \((R, \phi, z)\). The arc length is \(ds^2 = dR^2 + R^2 d\phi^2 + dz^2 = R^2 d\phi^2 + dz^2\). Minimize the integral \(\int \sqrt{R^2 + (z')^2} d\phi\).





If the functional depends on multiple functions \(y_1(x), y_2(x), \dots, y_n(x)\), \[ S = \int_{x_1}^{x_2} f(y_1, \dots, y_n, y_1', \dots, y_n', x) \, dx \] we can vary each function independently. This leads to a system of \(n\) independent Euler-Lagrange equations: \[ \frac{\partial f}{\partial y_i} - \frac{d}{dx} \frac{\partial f}{\partial y_i'} = 0 \quad \text{for } i = 1, 2, \dots, n \]
This extension is crucial for Lagrangian mechanics in 3D space, where we have coordinates \(x(t), y(t), z(t)\), and time \(t\) plays the role of the independent variable.

Problem 6.22 (Fermat’s Principle): Fermat’s principle states that light travels between two points along the path that requires the least time. Show that this leads to Snell’s Law \(n_1 \sin\theta_1 = n_2 \sin\theta_2\) for light crossing a boundary between media with refractive indices \(n_1\) and \(n_2\). Hint: Time \(t = \int \frac{ds}{v} = \int \frac{n(y)}{c} \sqrt{1+y'^2} dx\). Use the Beltrami identity since \(f\) doesn’t depend on \(x\).


Summary The calculus of variations allows us to find stationary paths for functionals. The fundamental tool is the Euler-Lagrange equation, which converts a global variational problem into a local differential equation. This mathematical foundation is what allows us to formulate Lagrangian mechanics based on Hamilton’s Principle of stationary action.

Learning Outcomes
By the end of the course students will be able to: 1. Identify and define the basic vocabulary used in Lagrangian and Hamiltonian Mechanics, and employ related variational methods to the study of mechanical systems. 2. Apply the fundamental principles of Classical Mechanics to the description of systems in noninertial frames of reference and to the analysis of the motion of rigid bodies. 3. Develop and implement problem-solving strategies useful in the analysis of examples and questions related to the description, behaviour, and evolution of mechanical systems. 4. Identify the main ideas and core physical principles in Classical Mechanics, and demonstrate their knowledge through deliberate time management and reflective judgement of the questions and problems in tutorial work, tests, and the final exam. 5. Review and update the mathematical toolbox of quantitative and analytical skills relevant and useful in the scientific endeavour in general and to the study of Physics in particular.
